newsitem.title: HAITI: Killings surge in Haiti as elections near.
newsitem.headline: Killings surge in Haiti as elections near.

text.p: A surge of violence has hit Haiti as the government faces simmering discontent from an impoverished and frustrated population.
Killings and shootings have marred the run-up to elections for the senate and district assemblies on Sunday, part of the island's drive for political stability after decades of dictatorship.

The bloodshed has also highlighted the shortcomings of the Haiti National Police force, which was set up to replace the repressive and corrupt military dissolved in 1995 after a U.S. invasion restored former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power the previous year.
Most murders appeared to be criminal acts as gangsters, known in Creole as "zenglendo", fought for control of slum areas. But some political figures have also been targeted.
On Saturday an Algerian policeman serving in the United Nations mission here was shot in the arm in the vast, fetid slum of Cite Soleil as gunfire rattled out there yet again.

U.N. spokeswoman Patricia Tome said about 50 people had been killed in February and March, including eight policemen, although the exact number was hard to say because of the varying reasons for the violence.

Fighting between rival gangs exploded in Cite Soleil in February with pitched battles in the streets in which at least 18 people died. The clashes subsided after police and U.N. peacekeepers intervened but random murders have continued.
In March the Justice Ministry's security chief was killed at a busy intersection in broad daylight and a senator was shot and wounded in the head.
"It's bad here everyday. It never changes," a U.N. police officer, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters at the crumbling police station amidst of the filth of Cite Soleil.

Gangs with names like Base Big-up and Base Maniac were involved in drugs, theft and robbery and had impressive arsenals. Some had emerged from underground militias formed during the dark days of military rule.
"Now the oppressed have become the oppressors," he said.
The U.N. special represenative in Haiti, Enrique Ter Horst, said on Wednesgay he did not believe the violence threatened Haiti's political stabilty.
He said there was a mood of uncertainty and impatience with President Rene Preval's government but that spurts of violence "come and go" in Haiti.

"There is some suspicion in the minds of some that it is poltical but I don't see it. Some are perhaps taking advantage of it but with the exception of a few cases I don't see it as political, he told Reuters.
HNP spokesman Felder Jean-Baptiste said police had gained control of the situation with the arrest of 15 gang leaders.

But the police themselves have come in for criticism over their conduct. Human Rights Watch said in a report released in January the HNP was inexperienced and lacked training and equipment. It also charged that some officers were practising torture and summary killings.
Accompaning the violence has been a series of strikes called by grassroots organisations who say the government has has failed to improve the lives of Haiti's ranks of poor.

They have threatened to use violence to enforce them and although a strike last month passed without bloodshed, the slogan of one group -- "Koupe Te, Boule Key", Creole for "cutting heads, burning houses", the rallying cry of the 1805 slave revolt -- did little to alleviate the fearful mood.
